evidence_items.excerpt: necessity: if [p] is fully grounded in D, then □(∧D → p). The thesis concerns full grounds and the modal entailment of the grounded proposition by the full ground propositions.
evidence_items.overview: This formula is the article’s target proposition. It fixes the relevant sense of necessary grounding as modal entailment from full grounds, rather than as a claim that the grounding relation itself or some grounding relation must recur in every possible world.
evidence_items.title: Necessity Thesis Formula

evidence_items.excerpt: Two shortcuts are rejected: causation is a determination relation without iii-style necessity, and necessary truths can have merely partial grounds despite trivially satisfying □(∧D → p).
evidence_items.overview: The passage motivates the need for a deeper argument. It shows that neither a broad taxonomy of determination relations nor a purely modal definition of full grounding explains why full grounds necessitate what they ground.
evidence_items.title: Failed Modal Shortcuts

evidence_items.excerpt: significance: [p] is fully grounded in D only if the connecting questions with respect to [p] and D lack cognitive significance.
evidence_items.overview: This principle supplies the epistemic constraint on grounding. It says that genuine full grounding excludes an in-principle explanatory gap of the relevant connecting-question kind, while leaving ordinary subject-relative ignorance out of the grounding fact itself.
evidence_items.title: Significance Principle

evidence_items.excerpt: essence: lack of cognitive significance requires essential truths characteristic of [p], D, their plurality, or involved entities according to which ∧D → p.
evidence_items.overview: This principle links the epistemic absence of a live connecting question to Fine-style essence. It explains why the ground propositions imply the grounded proposition: the implication is written into the nature of the relevant facts, plurality, or entities.
evidence_items.title: Essence Entailment Principle

evidence_items.excerpt: Formal chain: assume [p] is fully grounded in D; significance removes cognitive significance; essence supplies essential truths for ∧D → p; essential truths are metaphysically necessary; so □(∧D → p).
evidence_items.overview: The proof step integrates the article’s two substantive principles with the modal status of essential truths. It is the central argumentative bridge from an epistemic condition on grounding to the modal necessity of full grounding.
evidence_items.title: Five-Step Necessity Proof

evidence_items.excerpt: Alleged failures of necessity are diagnosed by adding missing explanatorily relevant facts for partial grounds, or by denying that the alleged ground is a ground at all.
evidence_items.overview: The conclusion protects the necessity thesis against cases involving enabling conditions, universal generalizations, widowhood, and substance-mode dependence. The response limits the thesis to full grounds and rejects cases where explanatory relevance is absent.
evidence_items.title: Counterexample Diagnosis

relations.rationale: The significance principle supplies the first substantive premise in the proof that grounding is necessary.
The essence principle supplies the essential-truth bridge from cognitive insignificance to entailment.
The integrated proof directly establishes the article’s necessity thesis for full grounding.
The counterexample diagnosis defends the necessity thesis by preserving the distinction between full grounds, partial grounds, and non-grounds.
Paradigm grounding cases motivate treating cognitive insignificance as a general constraint on grounding.

sections.body: The article’s central thesis is not that grounding is a modal relation in every possible respect, but that full grounds necessitate what they ground. Formally, when [p] is fully grounded in D, the conjunction of propositions corresponding to D metaphysically entails p. This makes necessity a constraint on complete explanations rather than on every partial explanatory factor.
sections.heading: Target Thesis

sections.body: Trogdon rejects two quick routes to the conclusion. A determination-relation argument is too broad because causation can determine without the relevant necessity. A definitional route is also unstable because necessary truths can have partial grounds that satisfy modal entailment trivially. The necessity thesis therefore needs a non-circular explanation.
sections.heading: Why Shortcuts Fail

sections.body: The significance principle introduces the epistemic constraint: full grounding rules out a cognitively significant connecting question. If a suitably informed rational subject could still find it substantively open why [p] obtains given D, then D has not supplied a full ground for [p]. Paradigm logical grounding cases are used to motivate this generalization.
sections.heading: Cognitive Significance

sections.body: The essence principle explains why the connecting question disappears. On the Finean picture, real definitions or essential truths disclose what the relevant facts and entities are. When those truths include or entail ∧D → p, grasping the natures involved makes the connection intelligible rather than arbitrarily modal.
sections.heading: Essence Link

sections.body: The proof combines the two principles with the necessity of essential truths. Full grounding gives cognitive insignificance; cognitive insignificance points to essential truths by which D entails p; and essential truths hold metaphysically necessarily. The result is □(∧D → p), which is the article’s target form of grounding necessity.
sections.heading: Necessity Argument

sections.body: Because the account uses epistemic notions, the paper addresses whether grounding becomes subjective. The answer is no: the relevant condition is about general epistemic facts concerning rational subjects who meet idealized information conditions. It is not about what any actual person happens to know, wonder, or be able to process.
sections.heading: Objectivity Concern

sections.body: The final section treats apparent counterexamples as diagnostic tests for explanatory completeness. Some cases omit enablers, totality facts, or marriage facts that are needed for full grounding. Another case involving a rose and its redness is treated more strongly: the alleged substance ground is not even a partial ground of the mode’s existence.
sections.heading: Counterexample Strategy

source_dossier.summary_long: The source develops a metaphysical argument for the thesis that full grounding is necessary: if [p] is fully grounded in D, then it is metaphysically necessary that the conjunction of the propositions corresponding to D entails p. Trogdon first separates this target from weaker or different modal ideas, such as the thought that the same grounding relation must hold whenever the grounds obtain, or that some grounded fact must result whenever the grounds obtain. The argument is needed because two tempting shortcuts fail. Grounding cannot simply inherit necessity from being a determination relation, since causation is plausibly a determination relation without the relevant modal force. Nor can full grounding be defined as grounding plus modal entailment, because necessary truths can have merely partial grounds that satisfy entailment trivially. The positive argument turns on two principles. The significance principle says full grounding requires the relevant connecting question to lack cognitive significance: once the relevant nature of the facts and entities is understood, the question why [p] obtains given D should no longer remain a substantive explanatory demand. The essence principle then says that this absence of cognitive significance is explained by Fine-style essential truths characteristic of [p], D, their plurality, or the entities involved, and those truths yield ∧D → p. Since essential truths are metaphysically necessary, the grounded proposition follows necessarily from the full grounds. The paper treats this epistemic vocabulary as compatible with objective grounding because the constraint concerns general facts about what questions could have substantive content for rationally informed subjects, not the ignorance of a particular person. In closing, Trogdon considers counterexamples involving moral reasons and enablers, universal facts, widowhood, and substance-mode dependence. The response is that the first group omits additional explanatorily relevant facts needed for full grounding, while the substance-mode case misidentifies a non-ground as a ground. The resulting picture is that grounding has modal consequences because essence closes the relevant explanatory gap.
source_dossier.summary_short: Kelly Trogdon’s article asks whether grounding is necessary in the sense that full grounds metaphysically entail what they ground. It answers yes, arguing from a constraint on cognitively significant connecting questions and a Fine-style account of essence. The paper also explains why familiar counterexamples are best treated as partial-ground or non-ground cases rather than failures of necessity.

summary: Kelly Trogdon argues that full grounding is necessary: whenever [p] is fully grounded in D, the propositions corresponding to D metaphysically entail p. The argument relies on an epistemic significance constraint and a Fine-style essence principle, then answers apparent counterexamples by distinguishing full grounds from partial grounds and non-grounds.
